raw_response:
I would start with Wiby and Marginalia for topic searches, then use personal directories and people's own links to keep exploring. For the kind of material you describe, the useful distinction is between living personal websites and preserved historical pages: both can reveal someone's sustained interest, but they serve different research needs.

1. **[Wiby](https://wiby.me/)** is the closest direct match. Its own description centers on hobbyist, academic and personally motivated pages that can be buried beneath commercial results. Search for a narrow subject from your research and use promising pages as starting points. Its selective index is a discovery aid, so a simple-looking page should not automatically be treated as old or authoritative. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn553738099view0"}}

2. **[Marginalia Search](https://marginalia-search.com/)** explicitly prioritizes non-commercial content and offers both search and exploratory discovery using its own crawler and index. It is another useful way to search for an obscure subject and encounter sites beyond the familiar large destinations. Non-commercial priority does not guarantee that every result is independent or reliable. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn553738099view1"}}

3. **[Neocities Browse](https://neocities.org/browse)** gives you a public directory of personal sites with interest tags. The site's public implementation also supports random and recently updated ordering, which can make browsing more productive than repeatedly visiting the most prominent sites. Try a hobby tag, open several pages, and follow their links. Many of these are present-day creations, so use them for the living personal web rather than assuming they are historical survivals. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn553738099view2","turn985673302view0"]}}

4. **[Ye Olde Blogroll](https://blogroll.org/)** is a human-curated directory of personal and independent blogs, organized into subjects including art, daily life, outdoor interests, and science and humanities. It is useful when you want someone's continuing writing and interests across a broader range of topics. The directory discloses sponsorship, and each linked blog still needs to be judged on its own merits. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn760868873view0"}}

5. **[The Wayward Webring](https://waywardweb.org/)** collects people's link collections. That makes it a starting point for the old habit of following one person's carefully chosen links into another person's interests. Its directory includes small-web resources, fan interests, creative work and many other subjects. The page I inspected was updated on November 19, 2026, after your April 4 question date, so I cannot treat its current membership as an April snapshot. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn760868873view1"}}

6. **[tilde.town](https://tilde.town/)** provides a community-oriented route. Its homepage links public member pages and projects from a shared-server community devoted to art, socializing and learning. It may be especially appealing if you enjoyed the sense of people making things for one another, although it represents a particular computing-oriented community rather than all kinds of enthusiasts. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn760868873view3"}}

7. **[The GeoCities Gallery](https://geocities.restorativland.org/)** is useful if the book research needs actual earlier personal websites. It organizes restored archived sites by subject neighborhoods, including literature, science, fandom and family life. Its own changelog dates the initial release to January 2019. Treat the pages as restored historical evidence: some files or outgoing links may be missing, and this is not evidence of an active present-day community. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn553738099view4"}}

My suggested browsing method is to choose one narrow interest, find a page whose author has clearly spent time on it, and then follow its links, blogroll or related-site list. Those selections can lead to a more personal trail than another broad search. For book research, record the individual page's URL and visible dates separately from the date of the directory that led you there.

I verified the primary pages above as current sources. Most were undated live pages, so I have not established their exact state on April 4, 2026. The public GitHub code-search endpoint failed; the Neocities code was subsequently found through web search and opened directly. The broader tildeverse homepage was also blocked, so the community recommendation above rests on tilde.town's own accessible page.
